lines.note: The left running header is M ANTES DO I., with particularly weak strokes in the T and the separate DO I. The surviving letters and clear repeated right header support the incorporated reading, rather than the garbled OCR N ANES D.

Misucaxi means seeing through something; the initial is M, not OCR X, and the past ending is aita. This ordinary entry begins the page after the previous catchword Miſuca-; there is no enlarged initial to encode.

runs.text: hũa parte a outra. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: The literal definition is seeing from one side to the other, followed by a metaphorical use. Fitono begins the Japanese example; the Portuguese nasal abbreviation hũa is retained and the physical row is indented.

The Japanese describes seeing through a person's inner heart or breast. Enlargement favors a worn upward-pointing circumflex over the first o, qiôchǔuo, contrasting with the clear downward-pointing mark over u; the o accent remains a nonblocking weak-impression reading. The final pe- continues below.
Pe-netrar completes the metaphor of penetrating someone's breast. The scan has peito, including a faint i, not OCR peto; a second Japanese example then begins with the interior of a fortress.

runs.text: Ver o que paßa na fortaleza.

lines.note: Misucasu completes Xirono vchiuo and is translated as seeing what happens in the fortress. The printed paßa and fortaleza are preserved; this is an inset continuation, not a new headword.
Misumaxi means seeing well or perfectly. The scan shows the i in aita, omitted by the OCR ata; perfeita- is the printed line division and continues with mente below.
The single-word continuation completes perfeitamente. Its inset placement is restored, and it is not treated as a standalone entry or margin text.

Misute concerns abandoning something after seeing it. The Portuguese verb reads Deſemparar with m; the final al is visibly unhyphenated in this row even though the word continues below, so no expected hyphen is supplied.

Gũa completes the preceding al, and the definition continues with leaving the thing and immediately returning. The scan supports joined deixandoa, not OCR de ixandoa; an ink blot partly affects the ampersand, whose upper strokes remain visible.

Mit is explained by fisoca, 'secret'; the synonym has c, not the OCR t in Fiſota. The example Mitni mǒ- preserves the bare final t of the headword and the visible caron over o before the divided verb.
ſu completes mǒ-ſu, 'to speak,' in the preceding example. The Portuguese gives speaking in secret and remains separate from the roman Japanese continuation.
Mitagaye is glossed briefly as erring while seeing. The printed g and the uru, eta paradigm are retained without replacing them by a modern Japanese spelling or conjugation.
The headword is Mitani with n, not OCR Mitari, and is explained by fucai tani, a deep valley. The P. label is italic, i, and the Japanese synonym are roman, and bai- continues on the next row.
Xo completes bai-xo, followed by fundo, 'deep'; the scan's n corrects OCR fuido. The entire row is Portuguese italic, including the initial x that was outside the draft's italic span.
Mitate is defined as finding or discovering by looking. The printed tçuru paradigm is retained and the final a- begins achar, rather than an independent preposition.
Char completes achar with the eyes; the paragraph mark introduces finding a site for a fortress. Xirono toco- remains a Japanese example with its visible end-of-row hyphen.
Rouo completes tocoro with the object particle; the verb is mitatçuru, not the OCR miratçuru. Its partially worn t matches the Mitate entry and the Portuguese finding or discovering a location.

runs.text: char lugar pera afortaleza. ¶ Item, Ir de

lines.note: The first example ends with finding a place for the fortress. A second sense begins after Item; the locally joined afortaleza and the phrase Ir de are retained rather than respaced or reordered.

runs.text: tras acompanhando os hoſpedes quando ſe tor-

lines.note: This sense describes following behind guests as they depart. The source has unaccented tras and hoſpedes, and the final tor- continues the verb below.

runs.text: não, ou leuar a alguem diante.

lines.note: Não completes tor-não, after which an alternative describes taking someone ahead. The historical leuar and alguem remain literal, and the paragraph ends here.
Mitçu is the honey entry, with its two-type tç sequence visibly present. The brief italic Mel is the complete gloss and is distinct from the preceding verb group.

Mitçubajeri names an herb; the definition does not identify a species beyond saying it is so called. The printed j and the ß of aßi are retained, rather than replacing the headword by a modern botanical spelling.

runs.text: Tres liſtras, ou riſcas que ſer-

lines.note: The headword denotes three stripes used as a mark or device. Its final iǒ includes a visible caron, and the definition's ſer- continues with uem on the next physical row.
Uem completes ſer-uem, explaining the stripes' use as an identifying emblem. Marca and diuiſa are Portuguese italic, with the historical u and long s left unchanged.

runs.text: Bacio grande de pao ẽ que

lines.note: The headword has Mitçu-, not OCR Mirçu-, and describes a large wooden tray or basin holding drinking cups. The Portuguese ẽ is a printed abbreviation and pao is left without an added nasal mark.

The tray holds three Sacazzuquis. The scan reads poem tres, correcting the OCR's poenutres; Sacazzuquis is an embedded Japanese cup-name printed in the surrounding italic and is listed for font review.
Mitçucuroi means looking out for or seeking something by observation. Both paradigm vowels carry circumflexes, and the Portuguese comma leaves the object or occasion to the next row.

runs.text: como ocaſião pera falar a alguem, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The illustrative object is an opportunity to speak with someone. The scan retains ocaſião and pera, then introduces the Japanese example with italic Vt,.

The example describes choosing a suitable time and calling someone. Iibunuo corrects the OCR Iibunuto; the weak mark in yobôzu is retained as a circumflex after comparison with the clear one in mitçucurôte, although its impression is incomplete.
This completes Vendo bõ tempo vos chamarei, 'I shall call you when I see a good time.' The abbreviated bõ belongs to the previous physical row and is not repeated here.
Mitçucuxi is seeing everything or exhausting the field of sight. The paradigm uita is preserved as printed rather than regularized, and eſgotar has long s, not an f.
The short continuation completes the expression 'exhaust with sight.' Its italic viſta and terminal period finish the entry without adding an object absent from the scan.
Mitçugui is aiding or assisting someone, rather than the tribute sense of a later noun. The g and the uida paradigm are legible, and italic Vt, introduces its example.

Nanguina tocoro identifies a difficult situation in which help is given. The roman Japanese ends mitçugu before the Portuguese Socorrer no; neither the example nor its individual words are embedded-font candidates.
The Portuguese completes helping in hardship or danger. Trabalho has weak internal strokes but the complete word is supported by the visible sequence and the paired perigo.

Mitçumeguiri denotes a three-cornered boring tool. The headword's t is lightly printed, but the tç sequence is consistent with its surviving type and neighboring mitçu entries; the Portuguese tres is unaccented.

Mitçumune is the back of a blade with the form described below. Catana and Vaquizaxi occur within the Portuguese explanation and are italic in the scan; both are listed for human font review, not treated as separate synonyms.

runs.text: que tem tres vincos, ou quinas.

lines.note: This specifies three ridges or angles on the blade's back. The words vincos and quinas are Portuguese, and the continuation ends the preceding weapon-related definition.
Mitçuqe means finding or discovering by sight. The scan supports q, not g, and the Portuguese ends with abbreviated cõ; its object phrase continues on the next row.
The short row completes cõ a vista. The local OCR short-s form vista is retained in this italic st combination rather than normalized to the long-s spelling elsewhere.
Mitçuqemono is a thing found, transparently connected to the preceding finding verb. The worn d of achada remains readable, and no gloss or additional punctuation is supplied.

This mitçuqimono concerns dues, tribute or revenue, not a found object. Enlargement does not cleanly separate the dark terminal stroke of rendimẽ from a possible hyphen, so the locally aligned unhyphenated reading is retained rather than adding an expected mark; to continues below.

runs.text: to que ſe paga ao Rey.

lines.note: The revenue is paid ao Rey, 'to the king,' not OCR do Rcy. The scan shows the preposition ao and the complete Rey in italic; the erroneous roman c fragment is removed.

The headword describes a bent, hunched posture, with its printed double-u sequence retained. The Portuguese locally joins Oeſtar, uses alcorcouado, and divides dobra from do below without an assumed hyphen.

runs.text: do, ou encolhido, como velho. P.

lines.note: Do completes dobra-do and the gloss compares the bent or contracted posture to that of an old person. The concluding P. label belongs to the italic definition and does not create a new entry.

runs.text: Nome de hum rio por onde

lines.note: Mitçuxegaua names a river in the belief described below. The Portuguese preposition is por with a rounded o, not OCR par; no external geographical identification is inserted into the canonical text.

runs.text: dizem os gentios que paßão as almas na outra

lines.note: The definition attributes the passage of souls to what the gentios say, rather than stating it independently. The historical term and the ß in paßão are retained as printed.
This final left-column body row completes na outra vida, 'in the other life.' Its inset placement and period are clear above the bottom rule; it is not page furniture.
The right running header reads M ANTES DO I. The separate printed 162. at its far right has been assigned a fresh page-number ID rather than retained as garbled header letters.
The page number is 162., clearly printed at the far right of the running-header band. It is not part of the header wording.
The complete headword is Mitdan, not the OCR fragment indan, with a worn but surviving t before d. Fisocani cataru describes speaking secretly; the synonym begins Fi-, not the OCR Fa-.
This short Portuguese row completes speaking or treating a matter in secret. It is visibly inset and remains body text, not a second heading beneath the running header.
Mite is the filling verb, glossed Encher, distinct from the surrounding compounds meaning secret or unresolved. Its compact paradigm is retained as printed.

runs.text: Mitet. Imada touorazu. i, Texxezaru co-

lines.note: Mitet is explained as not yet having gone through or been fully settled, followed by Texxezaru co-. The headword ends in bare t, and the doubled x in Texxezaru and final word division remain literal.

runs.text: O não eſtar ainda a couſa determinada,

lines.note: To completes coto, then the Portuguese describes something not yet determined. The comma shows that the definition continues; the roman fragment to. is not absorbed into the italic prose.

The example prohibits speaking of unresolved matters. On enlargement the third letter of Miretna has an r-shaped shoulder with no secure surviving t ascender, so the local OCR Miretna is retained as a possible printed anomaly despite the headword Mitet and expected Mitetna; cotouo corrects cototo, and yǔna has a caron.

runs.text: Não digais couſas que não tendes ainda bem

lines.note: The Portuguese renders the prohibition as not saying things one has not yet properly ascertained. Both occurrences of não and the uncontracted tendes are preserved.
This completes the requirement that the matters be known and verified. The initial ſ of ſabidas and historical aueriguadas are preserved as printed.

runs.text: Nome ſecreto, & que não he ordina-

lines.note: The headword is Mitgǒ, with M, t and a caron, not the garbled Airgǒ. Its definition reads 'a secret name' and 'not ordinary,' correcting OCR ſareto and rão from the visible Portuguese.
Rio completes ordina-rio, followed by corrente, an ordinary or current name. The physical word division is kept rather than moving the fragment back to the preceding row.

Mitgui is glossed as a secret. Enlarged type supports the literal Cacuita coto, including the dotted i missing from OCR Cacuta; the cluster is not expanded to a more expected Japanese spelling where no additional printed letter is visible.
Mitguiǒ is explained as secret conduct or practice. Its final iǒ carries a caron; Fisocana voconai is a standalone Japanese paraphrase, while the Portuguese e- begins exercicios below.
Xercicios completes e-xercicios, works or exercises done secretly. The lack of a modern accent in exercicios is preserved and the entry ends with the printed period.
Mitji is a secret matter, explained by the locally joined Fisocanacoto. The bare t plus j spelling is not expanded, and the Portuguese ſe- continues into segredo below.
After completing ſe-gredo, the first example is telling or discussing secret matters. Mitjiuo cataru is roman Japanese; the Portuguese Praticar is kept in its historical conversational sense.
The translation finishes with recounting secrets, and a second example begins revealing a secret. Araua- ends with a visible hyphen and continues with ſu on the next row.
ſu completes araua-ſu in the second Mitji example, revealing a secret. The short Japanese continuation is roman, while both Portuguese long-s words remain italic.

Mitmit is an adverbial expression for secrecy, repeated as Mitmitni in the example rather than the OCR Nitmitni. A small raised hyphen is visible after mǒ at the right edge; it is retained with the divided verb and not confused with the caron over o.
This completes mǒ-ſu and translates the example as speaking secretly. The initial roman ſu. belongs to the Japanese verb rather than to the following italic Portuguese.
Mitocorodô describes a bow bound in three places, as specified below. The final o has an upward-pointing circumflex, and the Portuguese eſtà retains its grave.

The bow is wrapped with rota at three points; the example repeats Mitocorodô with the genitive no. Rota remains the source's material-name, and the Japanese compound is not split into newly normalized words.
Yumi completes the expression 'a mitocorodô bow.' The italic Idem refers back to the same object, and the isolated continuation is preserved as a physical row.
Mitogame means privately noting something objectionable in another person. The g and the uru, eta paradigm are clear; the Portuguese object is completed on the next row.

runs.text: de algũa falta, ou outra couſa que deſagra-

lines.note: The noticed matter is a fault or something else displeasing. The tilde is over u in algũa, and deſagra- visibly divides the Portuguese verb without altering its letters.
Da completes deſagra-da and ends the definition with &c. This short inset row is body text, not an omitted or independent entry.
Mitodoqe is seeing a matter through to the end. The scan reads tè, with a grave, correcting OCR eẽ; ocabo is locally joined, and Fi- begins the Japanese example on the next row.

Tono completes Fi-tono, and the example concerns observing a person's hardship through to the end. Xinrǒuo retains its caron and object sequence; the Portuguese repeats exactly tè ocabo as in the preceding row.

runs.text: o trabalho, & anguſtia com que hum paßa.

lines.note: The translation names the hardship and anguish a person undergoes. Hum and paßa retain their printed spellings, and no accent is supplied to anguſtia.

A second example is staying with one's master through to the end. Xujinuo is the roman object phrase, followed by italic Perſeuerar; the paragraph mark begins within the inset continuation rather than at the headword margin.

runs.text: o ſenhor àte o cabo nos ſeus trabalhos, doenças,

lines.note: This specifies remaining with the master through hardships and illnesses. The source's àte has the accent on a, unlike modern até, and is preserved with the separate o cabo here.
Exile is the final named adversity in the extended example. Deſterro is a Portuguese continuation with long s, followed by &c., not a new Japanese entry.

runs.text: Couſa que tenho aſco de ver, ou

lines.note: Mitomonai describes something one feels disgust at seeing, with another motivation given below. The headword's historical vowel sequence is preserved rather than replaced by a modern form.

runs.text: que ſe não pode ver por algum outro reſpeito.

lines.note: The alternative covers being unable to look at something for another reason. Reſpeito is Portuguese in the sense of consideration or reason, not an embedded Japanese term; the sentence ends before the two derivative rows.

This inset derivative names the quality associated with Mitomonai and has no printed Portuguese gloss. Enlargement shows an italic initial M followed by roman letters, contrasted with the wholly roman Mitomonǒ below; only that first glyph is marked italic.
This second inset derivative has a clear caron over its final o. It is a standalone Japanese form without a printed gloss and remains on its own physical row.

Mitono macubai is defined as copulation or union. The printed macubai spelling is retained without normalizing its consonants from a modern Japanese expression; the people concerned are specified below.
The union is that of the first Camis. Camis is embedded in Portuguese and printed in the surrounding italic, so it is listed for human font review rather than mistaken for a new Japanese example.
Mitore concerns being absorbed or entranced while gazing. Its initial M is weak at the left but recognizable; the local Estar spelling and historical enleuado are kept without modernization.

runs.text: os olhos fitos vendo algũa couſa.

lines.note: The definition specifies fixed eyes looking at something. The f in fitos is lexical f, unlike a long s, and algũa preserves the visible nasal mark over u.
Mitori is immediately grasping or learning something by seeing it. The u, otta paradigm includes doubled t; the Portuguese sentence continues rather than ending after aprender.
This completes learning something upon seeing it. The historically separate em a construction is retained and not converted into a modern contracted or infinitival form.
Mitouonoqi describes ceasing to see something for an extended time. The headword's printed uo sequence and qu ending are retained, while Portuguese cou- continues on the next row.

runs.text: ſa como liuro, amigos, & c. por muito tẽpo.

lines.note: ſa completes cou-ſa, with books and friends as examples of things not seen for a long time. The source abbreviates tẽpo and retains the historical liuro; the locally spaced & c. is not expanded.
Mitouoxi means penetrating or passing through with one's sight. The printed past ending is oita, and paßar keeps the source's ß rather than a modern ss.
This final phrase completes the preceding definition. The local short-s vista in the italic st combination is preserved rather than automatically changed to viſta.

The expression describes poison sweetened with honey. The scan separates Mit rino, with the t partly lost, and shows a small upward-pointing mark in fiſô; the circumflex is retained despite the lexical aid's caron and the different-looking mark in the following example.

The example wraps the poison in honey; the scan separates Mit rini, correcting OCR Mit aini. The worn accent in fiſǒuo is read as a caron from its heavy descending left side and faint rising right side, unlike the apparent circumflex above; both occurrence-specific readings remain caveated. The Portuguese translation continues beyond this page.
The bottom signature has a large S, a smaller lowercase s and the numeral 2. It is separate from the catchword at the far right; no letters of the Portuguese continuation belong to this signature.

The italic Portuguese catchword peço- anticipates the continuation of the unfinished translation on the following page. It is printed below the last body row and is not appended to the gathering signature.
